clue.text: Platitudes suit Mrs Batty

indicators.note: batty means crazy, so the letters are thrown into a mad new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses the tired sayings that please an eccentric old lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batty' reads like a surname for Mrs, but it is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Truisms are statements so obvious they hardly need saying, which is what platitudes are; the two are near synonyms.

clue.text: Cosily warm where pig may go?

blocks.note: first meaning: snug and pleasantly heated
second meaning, cryptic: the destination of a pig being sent to its pen, split into three short words

explanation.surface: A snug spot is wondered about as somewhere a pig might wander.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the wordplay is a playful phrase, TO A STY, run together into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Toasty is an informal adjective for pleasantly heated and comfortable, matching snug warmth.

clue.text: Invisible nun out to secure diocese

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so these letters are rearranged
to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: taken as written
a see is a bishop's diocese

explanation.surface: A nun goes about invisibly, out to grab control of a church district.
explanation.walkthrough: A bishop's see is his diocese, a standard crossword equivalence; the rearranged NUN splits around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unseen has not been observed, which is close in sense to invisible, not able to be viewed.

clue.text: Lush struggling with morals? One or two!

indicators.note: something struggling is twisting about, so the letters writhe into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drunkard wrestles with conscience, perhaps over whether to have one drink or two.
explanation.walkthrough: A lush is slang for a heavy drinker, and 'One or two' sounds like drinks; it means one o'clock or two o'clock in the morning.
explanation.definitionFit: The early-morning times just after midnight, such as one a.m. and two a.m., are examples of what this phrase names.

clue.text: Seconds for good child

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for seconds
pro means in favour of, i.e. for
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A well-behaved youngster is rewarded with second helpings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like a link word but supplies PRO, Latin-derived for 'in favour of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprog is British slang for a youngster or small offspring, a jokey informal word for a kid.

clue.text: See 11
Killer in cowboy film avoiding northern city

indicators.note: to avoid something is to keep it out, so a letter is dropped
one piece sits inside another, as the word plainly says

blocks.note: a Western is a film about cowboys
N is the abbreviation for northern, the letter removed
an orc is a killer whale

explanation.surface: A gunslinger in a Western deliberately rides around a city in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Killer' suggests a gunfighter, but it is the killer whale, ORC; the film loses its N and wraps round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Worcester is a cathedral city in the English Midlands, the county town of Worcestershire.

clue.text: Letter from Greek written up in Conservatoire

indicators.note: the letters sit inside a longer word of the clue
in a down entry, writing upward means the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the run of letters near the end of the word

explanation.surface: A letter from a Greek student is posted up at a music school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter from Greek' reads as correspondence, but it is a letter of the Greek alphabet; a conservatoire is a music college.
explanation.definitionFit: Iota is the ninth character of the Greek alphabet, equivalent to the Roman i.

clue.text: Reportedly game working for poet

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than read, so we go by sound

blocks.note: tennis is a game and on means working

explanation.surface: A sports fixture is said to be going ahead for a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: ON for working is a common crossword equivalence, as a machine that is on is running.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was a Victorian Poet Laureate, author of The Charge of the Light Brigade.

clue.text: Freedom from pain having absorbed ultimate enzyme

indicators.note: what has been absorbed is now inside, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: ease is relief from discomfort
ultimate means final

explanation.surface: Pain relief comes from having taken in an important enzyme.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a medical claim, but the first three words are simply one synonym that opens to hold the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Elastase is a protein-digesting chemical catalyst in the body that breaks down elastin.

clue.text: Bewildered, take a satnav around periodically

indicators.note: periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept
turning around faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the even letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A lost driver is told to bring a satnav along on the next trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The satnav suggests being lost on the road, which suits the definition nicely; only every second letter counts.
explanation.definitionFit: Being at sea is an idiom for being confused and unsure what to do, like a ship without bearings.

clue.text: Queen Mother departing African country for imaginary one

indicators.note: what departs leaves its place, making room for something else
for means instead of, so one piece stands in place of another

blocks.note: R is short for Regina, Latin for queen
ma is an informal word for mother, the piece that leaves
a country in north-west Africa

explanation.surface: The Queen Mother leaves a real African state for a fairy-tale realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen Mother' looks like one royal figure but splits into two pieces: R comes in where MA leaves the start of Mauritania.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruritania is the fictional central European kingdom of The Prisoner of Zenda, a made-up nation.

clue.text: Show why this dole letter gets shredded

indicators.note: shredding tears into pieces, so the letters are cut up and reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A demonstration of why an unemployment benefit letter ends up in the shredder.
explanation.walkthrough: Every letter of the five words before 'shredded' is used; the dole is British unemployment benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a long-running BBC television music programme of the 1970s and 80s, so it is a broadcast programme.

clue.text: Maybe boil some spicy stew

indicators.note: some means only part of, so the letters lie within the words

blocks.note: spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A cook might bring some of a spicy stew to the boil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boil' looks like a cooking verb, but 'Maybe boil' is a noun definition: a boil is an example of a skin swelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A cyst is a sac-like swelling under the skin; a boil is loosely an instance of such a lump.

clue.text: Local artist, notorious lord and clergyman, retired

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: RA is a Royal Academician
Lord Lucan vanished in 1974 after his children's nanny was murdered
Rev is short for reverend

explanation.surface: A local painter, an infamous peer and a vicar have all retired.
explanation.walkthrough: RA, a member of the Royal Academy, is the standard crossword artist; Lord Lucan is a British aristocrat who disappeared after a murder.
explanation.definitionFit: Vernacular describes the everyday language or style of a particular region, so as an adjective it means native or regional.

clue.text: Old man leading show?

blocks.note: first meaning: a father, or pop, who is ahead of all other fathers
second meaning: a long-running BBC music chart programme

explanation.walkthrough: Pop is an informal word for father, so the dad in front is the best of all of them; the same phrase names the BBC chart show.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase was the title of the BBC weekly chart television programme, and literally describes the foremost of all dads.

clue.text: University student coming in cheers monthly event

indicators.note: what comes in enters, so these letters go inside another word

blocks.note: U is the abbreviation for university
L is a learner, the plate on a student driver's car
an ovation is a burst of applause and cheering

explanation.surface: A university student arrives to cheers at a monthly party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'student' is L because British learner drivers display an L plate; 'cheers' looks like a toast but is applause.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovulation, the release of an egg from the ovary, happens roughly once each menstrual cycle, about every four weeks.

clue.text: Get together in Ulster assembled on high ground

indicators.note: assembled things are put together in a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
up means on higher ground, elevated

explanation.surface: People meet up in Northern Ireland, gathering on a hillside.
explanation.walkthrough: Ulster is the northern province of Ireland; 'Get together' is the definition, though it reads like the gathering in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To rustle up is to gather or put something together quickly, such as a meal or a group of helpers.

clue.text: Perhaps saw advantage raising money

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising lifts the letters so they read bottom to top

blocks.note: an edge is an advantage over a rival
loot is slang for money

explanation.surface: Someone may have spotted a chance to make some cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saw' reads as the past tense of see, but it is the cutting implement, an example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is one example of a tool with a cutting blade, so it is an instance of the category.

clue.text: French and German articles present latent suspicion

blocks.note: un is the French for a
der is the German for the
current means present, happening now

explanation.surface: Foreign news pieces hint at a hidden mistrust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'articles' covers both foreign words: the indefinite article in French and the definite one in German.
explanation.definitionFit: An undercurrent is a hidden feeling or tendency running beneath the surface, such as unspoken distrust.

clue.text: Actress and singer playing role, at first

blocks.note: a part is an actor's role
on means performing, playing on stage
a placing instruction: the word for role goes in front

explanation.surface: A performer who both acts and sings takes a role at the start of her career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' tells you the role-word goes in front of the word for playing.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolly Parton is the American country music star who has also acted in films such as 9 to 5.

clue.text: Unqualified one must abandon English course

indicators.note: to abandon is to leave, so a letter departs the word

blocks.note: entire means complete, without qualification
I is the Roman numeral one, removed
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A student without qualifications has to drop an English course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' suggests study, but it is a course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: An entree is a dish served as part of a meal, the main dish in America or one before it in Britain.

clue.text: Fall heavily where hunting party returns

indicators.note: returning goes back the way one came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a meet is a gathering of riders and hounds for a hunt

explanation.surface: A rider takes a nasty tumble where the hunt comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall heavily' reads as a rider's tumble, but it is rain pouring down.
explanation.definitionFit: When rain teems it pours down in torrents, so the verb means to come down hard as precipitation.

clue.text: Drinking tea, future bride at home in floral arrangement

indicators.note: what drinks takes something in, so one piece is swallowed by another

blocks.note: Daisy is asked to marry in the song Daisy Bell, 'give me your answer, do'
someone at home is in
cha is a slang word for tea

explanation.surface: A bride-to-be sips tea at home among the flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: The future bride is Daisy of the music-hall song Daisy Bell, being proposed to; she and IN together take in the tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A daisy chain is a string of the little flowers linked by their stems, a simple garland.

clue.text: Barely enough time to finish examination

blocks.note: a scan is a medical examination
T is the abbreviation for time
a placing instruction: the letter for time goes at the end

explanation.surface: A student has hardly any time left to complete a test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'examination' suggests a school test, but it is a medical scan.
explanation.definitionFit: Scant means scarcely sufficient, so the adjective names an amount that only just suffices.

clue.text: See 11
Oresteia somehow packs in 100 mysterious items

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are arranged afresh
to pack something in is to stuff it inside

blocks.note: taken as written: the trilogy by Aeschylus
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Aeschylus's Greek tragedy trilogy is somehow crammed with a hundred obscure references.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oresteia is a set of three ancient Greek tragedies by Aeschylus; its title supplies all the letters except the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoterica are things understood only by a select few, obscure and arcane matters or objects.

clue.text: Left devoured Right in show

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
ate is the past tense of eat, as devoured is
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: In a political debate programme, the Left tears apart the Right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devoured' looks like a container signal but just gives ATE; Later... with Jools Holland is a BBC music programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Later, hosted by Jools Holland, is a long-running BBC television music series featuring live performances.

clue.text: Speed ahead to keep old cyclists in group

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: to pelt is to run very fast
on as in going on ahead, forward
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A racer speeds ahead while veteran riders stay bunched together.
explanation.walkthrough: The racing scene is apt: the wordplay reads like a breakaway, and the answer is the bunch left behind.
explanation.definitionFit: The peloton is the main pack of riders bunched together in a road race such as the Tour de France.

clue.text: Dramatist runs into youngster by church

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
a teen is a teenager
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A playwright bumps into a young person beside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: Terence was a Roman comic playwright of the second century BC; CE stands for Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Terence, Publius Terentius Afer, wrote Latin comedies, so he is a classical playwright.
